We now see that a lot of her answers, for example, are of no particular value because they do not deal with the issues you want to, although they are clearly matters which the witness herself thinks are relevant to your questions. I don't want to be seen to be criticising either of you, you or the witness, but it was becoming difficult for us to understand just where it was we were going. You have been of great assistance in explaining why it is you have taken this line, and you proceed with it in what way you see fit. The circumstances in which you have been called upon to deal with this witness are such that I would not stop you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Madam, would you be kind enough when it comes to questions and answers, please to make pauses because of the interpretation so that our performance should be a bit better than it was this morning. Speaking about the day when you were in front of the Vuk Karadzic School and inside the school, you frequently mentioned the Vuk Karadzic School and inside the school, you frequently mentioned a person that you appear to know well, Miloje. Could you tell us who that person was and what he was doing on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: Yes, [redacted] in the village into which I had married.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And what is his surname?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: Joksimovic. I even took some of my things to his place and he helped to do that. I wanted to burn them, and he says, "Madam, don't do that. You can bring whatever you like over here and leave them here." "My house is small," he said, "but there is a house next door that hasn't been completed yet and you can leave everything in there."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Tell me, please, this person, this Miloje Joksimovic, did he come when you were in front of the school and in the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: Yes, he brought my mother-in-law and father-in-law and he looked -- he went to look for transport for us to Belgrade, and he came back immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did he come back afterwards, when the person who was making those records that you identify as Mitar was still there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: No. He didn't. Mr Ristic came and he told me -- he didn't call me Madam. He called me by name, and he said I should take my mother-in-law inside because Miloje hasn't managed to get transport for you. A problem has arisen between your people and our people, and he still hasn't come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So that means that you were expecting Miloje to provide transportation and that is why you stayed outside, and you thought that you would be leaving by special transport?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And you told us that this Ristic was there, too. Who is Ristic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: I didn't know him well but he was a relative of Miloje's. I think his grandmother was from the Joksimovic family. I know the Ristics well. There was a Ristic who went to school with me, and I asked him which Ristic he was. He told me his name. He told me his name but I don't remember it. His nickname was Gara -- Gaga, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you don't know his real name. You know he was Ristic known as Gaga?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: He gave me his name but I haven't remembered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: This Ristic, was he there at the same time as the person you have identified as Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: No. He went off with Miloje. He drove. Ristic drove the Niva car.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But you said he returned before Miloje and told you that Miloje is unable to provide transportation, so they didn't go together?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: They left together but they didn't come back together. Ristic came back alone. Miloje did not come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you please tell me this? When you were telling us how close you were to this book in which the names were being entered, and I think you said that he leafed through the book until he found a clean page. Does that mean that there were other entries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: I don't know whether there were two or three pages, whether -- I didn't read what was on it, whether there were names or something else. But I did see it with my own eyes, just as I'm looking at the screen. He leafed two or three pages over and then he found a clean page and started writing down names, the names of my neighbours from the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember, on this clean piece of paper, whether there were ordinal numbers, 1, 2, 3, 4, and what was actually entered in the book in addition to the first and last name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: I didn't notice anything else, whether there were numbers 1, 2, 3 or 5. Just as people gave their names, I saw him writing them down. Because I didn't stand there all the time. As somebody was entered, I would go and help those people to carry in their things if they were elderly or weak or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Madam, I'm going to have to ask you to restrain yourself again. Please wait before you start your answer. It's terribly important. Otherwise, we are going to lose what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I hope that that isn't because you're having so much trouble.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No, no, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: There was a Cira from Loznica who saw him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But we didn't have the translation of the question either.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I will repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because of the interpretation which is missing, let me repeat the question. Could you tell me the name of another person who was present and who saw this person who you've identified as Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: Cira Dzuric. He was a police -- he was armed and Mitar was not armed. I mentioned him. Cira came with the convoy on the trucks with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: This Cira Dzuric, where was he from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: From the village of Loznica. He worked on the roads, repairing roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Apart from him, do you know the other persons who were there in the school? You mentioned somebody's nickname, Cacanin, I think?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: Yes, we found him there in front of the school, sitting at this small table when we arrived. He was sitting at the table. But I didn't know him from before at all. And there was somebody called Ivanovic from Paocici. He recognised me when he arrived in the convoy and he called me. My (redacted) And he said, "I saw your sister (redacted) when she left with her husband for Zepa. I was on guard and I let her pass and she is safe and well. Nobody hurt her." He's the only one I knew. I didn't know the others. This Cira and this Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell us anything more about this Ivanovic, his name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: I know that he's from the village of Paocici and his wife's name is Milica, and I've forgotten his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is his name perhaps Mirad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: There were three brothers, so I'd rather not say. I may get them mixed up. One of the brother’s name was Milorad. Whether it was his or his brother's, I'm not sure. Radenko and Milorad, I know those were the names of two brothers. I don't remember the third name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Throughout that time while you were there in the school and in front of the school, did you notice any of the policemen or any kind of security people in addition to those who came with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: No, just -- I did on one occasion only. A soldier came and introduced myself. I know he's from Foca. He entered the room where my family was and he pushed my father-in-law, "And you old people have gathered here, where are your extremists? They are all left in the woods." And ran out to look for Ristic or for Miloje to tell them what was going on. Then Ristic came and he said to this man from Foca, "Don't touch his family. This family is protected. Their son is in Belgrade." And then he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Since you mentioned this and you also mentioned the number of 119, they are women, children and elderly people; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does that mean that in these villages that you mentioned, Gostilja and the villages around, that at the time when you left for Visegrad, no men were left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: I will tell you but this will take some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, just answer my question, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: No. Because 64 able-bodied younger men went to Zepa. I went to the woods to collect them, when Rade Dikic came and Vukoman Pecencic, and they said, "By tomorrow, I will guarantee their lives if I find them here, but as of tomorrow, our army is coming. They are bringing dogs. They will set fire to the woods, and then no one's life will be safe."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And when was this in relation to this day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: It was the day before we left, and as soon as they left, I and another person who was at my mother-in-law's, while all the others were in the woods, I, too, spent one night in the woods, and then I came back the next day. I had left my mother-in-law alone. We couldn't carry her. She stayed behind, crying. And when I was bringing food to put it close to her so she would have something to eat, I didn't know whether I'd come back the next day. I thought I may not come back at all. And whatever I brought to the table for her, she threw it down. Then this woman put a bag of stuff on the table and she hit me with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Please don't go into such details. That was not my question. When you were talking about your visits to Visegrad, your visits to the market and going to restaurants and coffee bars, you said you did so with your husband?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: More often alone than with him. Sometimes if my husband was off-duty, he was with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Tell me this: Is it customary in the environment in which you lived, whether we are talking about Serbs or Muslims, for a woman to go to a coffee bar or to a restaurant alone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: Yes and no. Some went, some never. I did because my husband was a communist. He was not a hodza or a hajra, and I went to cafe bars alone but there were women who never entered a coffee bar alone, at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Talking about these women that didn't go to pubs, would it be right to say that they were in the majority?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: Yes, the majority. Only those whose husbands were communists would go to these pubs alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Madam, I was never a communist but my wife went.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: I'm talking about us villagers. Women from towns might go, yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's all right, Mr. Domazet. You are, I think, provoked into that. Madam, the court reporters are having a great deal of difficulty because of the speed at which you're speaking. So when you come to the end of a sentence or even a comma, may I suggest you also pause slightly. It is very important that we get all of this down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Madam, if I understood you correctly, [redacted] [redacted], did he not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: Yes. I can tell you this. He came for the weekend. He returned on the 1st of April. There were already barricades there and they were stopped. There were checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You also said today that after this day, that is the 22nd of April, 1992, that that was the last time you saw Mitar Vasiljevic. Let me ask you when, and under which circumstances, did you see him for the first time after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: I couldn't really tell you exactly, but I know when the first barricade was in front of his house, this must have been in March.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Madam, you're talking about the period prior to this. I'm talking about the period after the 22nd of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean, April of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, the 22nd of June. I'm sorry, my mistake.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: Yes, you've confused me. I don't know what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my mistake. You were talking about the 22nd of June as the last time that you allegedly saw Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic. My question is: After that, and before you saw him today in the courtroom, did you see him and when, in the newspapers, on television or -- and when did you hear that he had been arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: To tell you quite honestly, from Bosnia when I was speaking to my family members on the phone and they are in Sarajevo, they were the first to tell me. You know what's new? A man from our municipality was arrested today. He is such and such, that there was something in his house. I didn't know that. They told me that on the phone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, "that SFOR was in his house."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you heard that, did you remember that you had seen that person on that date in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I can say that. He didn't say anything bad to us in front of the school, and that is why I remembered. Because I would hear all kinds of things from others, doing much worse things than Mitar did. So I have nothing more to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What you're telling us about happened almost two years ago, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't know whether it is a year ago or two years ago. I don't know. I didn't pay any attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you learnt about this very soon after his -- he was taken into custody. My question is: How did it come about that you should be a Prosecution witness in this case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: When a team from here came to [redacted] to investigate, they came to see my son-in-law. His brother was taken away from the partizan company and while I was at the school, because my daughter had also left for Belgrade with her daughter, and then they called us on the TV and the radio, "We are calling the population of Visegrad to go back. If they don't come back, they will lose their jobs." And this son-in-law of mine came back, and in the bus, when he reached close to Visegrad, at the petrol station which is at the entrance to Visegrad, the bus was stopped there. There was a checkup and my son-in-law was taken out of the bus. My daughter held on to him and this man was pushing her away. In the meantime her colleague, I know her father's name was Burdus -- I don't know what her name was. She was the girlfriend of this young man who had taken my son-in-law, and she opened the door of a car and said, "Come with me. If you don't come with me now, I'll break off our relationship." But he didn't answer. I'm only taking him for half an hour to question him briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You must notice, Madam, that we have digressed considerably. My question is: How did it come about that you became a witness? You said a team came to [redacted] to investigate. When was this, please? Will you tell me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: That was last year in March. I don't remember the date. I didn't know I'd be coming here so I didn't make note of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So then on that occasion, did you personally, not other members of your family, did you give any kind of statement to investigators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I told them all of this that I have just told you and perhaps even five times more. My daughter -- I went to fetch my daughter, to bring her with me to Belgrade, and she gave a statement to investigators saying, "Perhaps my mother could tell you a bit more." My daughter stayed there perhaps just an hour or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: My question was: Did you give a statement? Did you give a statement? Did you sign a statement? Did you give any kind of statement on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: The only statement I gave was the one referring to who registered our names in front of the school, just as like -- as I told you here today. I don't know anything else. I didn't say anything else about these things that you asked me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if we understand each other well. Did you give a statement? Was that statement read to you? Did you sign that statement or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: I was given newspapers to look at, to see whether I could recognise anybody on those pictures. They put newspapers on the table, they spread them. I looked at the newspapers and I immediately recognised the person that registered our names, and then I signed my name over that person's forehead, and the man that led this -- conducted this interview, he signed his name below.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was that the photo spread that was shown to you today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: No. Well, yes. It wasn't the same picture. I also looked at a picture last year, and when I came here this time, I was given newspapers again to see if I could recognise somebody. And I again recognised Mitar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And was that the same photograph of his?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it was taken a bit later, because he looked chubbier to me than then. I don't know, but it's the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say "chubbier," what exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: Well, let me use a term we would use in our village: Fat. And by this, I mean his weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you are saying that there was a difference between those two pictures, that he was fatter on one picture?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: Well, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In addition to that occasion when you say various photographs were shown to you in March, and this other occasion, other than that, have you had a chance to see any other pictures of him or any TV footage of him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: No. Because I work in the second shift, and I really can't watch much TV. You know, I never come home before 10.00 or 10.30, so I really can't watch much TV. Other people have told me that they've seen him on TV but I personally didn't. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As you were telling us this, did you mean that this was taking place while you lived in [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: Yes. I couldn't go to Sarajevo for a long time. My whole family remained in Sarajevo. My father-in-law came back three years ago when we also had to come back and I spent that whole time in [redacted].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So that means that you lived in [redacted]. The fact that you travelled back home for vacation to Sarajevo is quite a different matter, but that whole time, you lived in [redacted]?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, let us summarise in a different way what you told us during last ten minutes just to make sure that we understood it well. So after the 22nd of June, 1992, you told us that you never saw Mitar Vasiljevic either in the papers or on TV, until the -- until March of 2001 - and please do not interrupt me - until that time when various photographs were shown to you and you believe that in those photographs, he was skinnier and different than on this photograph that you were shown today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: Yes. There was a slight difference there. He was somewhat skinnier, his hair style is the same. He simply looked thinner to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Since today, you are still telling us that the person you saw on the 22nd of June was Mitar. You identified him as Mitar, and you told us that this is the same person that you used to see in the preceding years in Vilina Vlas and so on. If he were to tell you that he never worked at the hotel in Vilina Vlas, would it in any way change your today's statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: I don't know. All I'm saying is that I used to see him personally in Vilina Vlas and that he used to wait on me. I said straight away that I used to see him less often on duty there. I said that at the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm telling you that he never worked there, and we can prove that. You claimed something different. I don't want to go into his whereabouts on the 22nd of June. I just wish to say the following, to ask you the following at the end: In addition to these problems of yours that you described, is there any other motive with respect to Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: No. I never saw him from the 4th of April up until that time when I registered our names in front of the school. I went around, I saw many people, but I never, ever saw Mitar in that time frame, and I can't say anything else other than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And why is it that you believe that this person that came to register names was in fact Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: Because I've known him since childhood. I can tell you that we were on the bus many times. He would get off on one bus before me to go and visit his wife's family, Milica, and I know this for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, Madam, perhaps you know this or you think that you know this but I'm telling you that he wasn't present there on the 22nd of June. I don't have further questions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: Thank you. If I'm not here now, then he wasn't there then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Madam, Mr. Domazet asked you about -- or you, in response to one of his questions, talked about a protection that you believed your family had and you talked about a certificate. My question to you is: Can you tell us, if you know, the name of the person who gave you that certificate which you believed protected you and your family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: It was Tomic, commander of the police station, SUP commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And Mr. Tomic, the commander of the SUP station, do you know his first name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, there were two brothers. We called them Tomic, just like they called me by my last name. Nobody used my first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So do you know the names of the two brothers or you don't know the names of either one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: I used to know them, but I forgot. I think that I passed him, this Tomic, many times. He came in a car and I was standing with my daughter and the young man that was with my daughter said, "Well, there goes Tomic," and that was the first time I saw him. I never saw him prior to that. And then I approached him. And prior to that I never went to the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Domazet has asked you about other people that you saw at the Vuk Karadzic School on the same day that you say you saw Mr. Vasiljevic. What I want to ask you is: Do you know a person by the name of Milan Lukic and did you see him present at the school on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: Well, to tell you that as well, I didn't know Milan Lukic by sight but I do know his parents well, because when I got married, Milan Lukic was six years old. My sister had a daughter and she was same age as him. They went to school together.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Ma'am, on the day that you were at the school, did anybody identify themselves as Milan Lukic to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: Two men came, Cira and another, in a police uniform. They came to the door. And they said, "Selam Aleykum." He said, "Where is Avdija Sabanovic? Where is Murat Sabanovic? May they all fuck you." And when he said all this to us, then he rolled his sleeve up and from on his police shirt, we could see it was written police, Milan Lukic, and then he introduced himself and said, "I am Milan Lukic, the greatest butcher in Visegrad. Take a good look at me. If you have a camera, take a picture of me. And then you can look at me when I go to Alija's state."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And this person who identified himself as Milan Lukic, did he say anything to the people regarding their property?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: No, nothing. He just brought a cardboard paper and then threw it on the floor in the middle of the hall, and said, "Everybody, all of you, if you have any metal items on you, put them on this paper here because we are going to search you. We had problems with a previous group that was here at school." Those were people from Zlijeb, and allegedly they had found a bomb among them. And our people started throwing various spoons, forks, small knives. Whatever they had, they started throwing on that piece of cardboard. And then I did that too. I took one of the spoons for myself because I'd forgotten to take with me when I left my house, and then he left for coffee.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Ma'am, can you estimate for us the time that elapsed between when Mitar Vasiljevic -- when you saw Mitar Vasiljevic leave and when in the day this person who identified himself as Milan Lukic arrived at the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: Well, yes, I can. Mitar left definitely before 12.00, and Milan Lukic came, it must have been after 4.00, because they came to tell me that we needed to go into the school because they did not find transport for us. So I entered the school shortly before Milan Lukic came to school.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you -- Mr. Domazet has asked you a number of questions regarding your certainty that this was -- that your observation was on the 22nd, and I want to ask you one or two questions regarding that before.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But before I do, I'm going to ask that Prosecution document 95, it will be a supplemental pseudonym sheet, that I'd ask that it be distributed to the Chamber and then to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: When you say a "substitute" one --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No. I said a supplemental one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So it will be Exhibit P95.1, and it will under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you were talking about the dates in response to questions Mr. Domazet was asking you, you testified that on the 14th, you were told that the people in your village had to leave on a convoy but that that did not occur. And then you were told -- you said you gathered at the school on the 22nd. So am I correct in saying that on the 21st -- on the 21st of June, once again you were told to prepare yourself to leave on a convoy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you to look at the sheet in front of you. The name of this person is protected, just as yours is, so I'll just ask you to refer to them by their number 18. In between the time that you saw or first were told -- please let me finish.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: If I'm able to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Please tell us, in between the time on the 14th, when you say you were first told you had to leave, and the time on the 22nd, when you were at the school, did you ever see this person, VG18?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: Yes. That person was the one who brought the major piece of news to us. That person came to our village, and then in this neighbouring village called Polje, women started crying. A daughter of one woman burnt in the fire. She was just a baby, perhaps 24 hours old. So this person went to see that mother first. And when we heard her -- when we heard somebody crying in front of that house, this woman was mourning for her daughter calling her "my little birdy," this daughter of hers, and somebody from their village, me and two more people, went immediately to that village of Polje - it is some 20 minutes away perhaps - and then when we got there, this woman was just walking around the house hitting herself and saying, "Brothers and sisters, go into mountains, go into water, but don't go outside. I don't have anybody here in my neighbourhood. They torched everybody. They burnt everybody yesterday." And then she told us, and they wrote down the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recall whether VG18 -- without telling the names of any people, did VG18, did she have anybody with her?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: Yes, her child. And this person said that Mitar Vasiljevic wrote down their names, that he took them to the house of Jusuf Memic in Pionirska Street and put them up there and gave them a sheet of paper saying, "This is safe for you. Nobody will touch you." They believed him. They believed it was going to be so. This encouraged them. And then they had dinner and went to bed, and then somebody knocked on the door. They opened the door, and somebody said, "We have to come in and have a talk with you." So they said that two people came in, collected all of their money and gold, and I don't know what else, and then, well, they remained there in that house. And then an hour or two later - at least this is how this lady described this to us - they came again and knocked on the door, and then said, "It is not safe for you here. Why don't we transfer you into another house where it will be safe for you?" And then all of those people collected their belongings. It was night-time. One of them went in front, one went to the right, one went to the left, and one was in the back, so nobody could escape from that column until they got to this other house where they put them up. This house had a roof. It was Adem Omeragic's house. I know where that house was. They opened the door for them. She didn't tell us who took them and put them up in that house. She said, "It was 11.00 in the evening. I couldn't see well who took us to that house and put us up there. As soon as we got into that house, all of a sudden there was a spark and there was smoke, and people started screaming. I was next to the window. I hit the window with my hand and the glass cracked but I was unable to break it completely. I simply collapsed by the window. And my child was with me. My child fell down by me, and I felt that two or three people skipped over me and left alive. And then -- and then after that, it calmed down, and then I started crawling, crawled across the road into a sewer, and I remained there until it started to dawn."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Ma'am --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think you have to get it made clear that this is what she's being told by VG18; that's the first thing. And the second thing is when, because she said it seems as if this was the day after the fire. When you asked her, "Between the 14th and the 22nd, did you see VG18," she just said yes without saying when.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to first ask you -- you're telling a story to us now and you're using the word "I." Are you telling us what VG18 told you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what is your best memory about the date upon when VG18 told you this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: I don't remember the date. I just know that it was after the 14th, because we were supposed to go on that day as well, and she told us, "You were lucky that you didn't go that day because you could have been set on fire on that day as well." But they told us they would come in week's time to fetch us, seven to eight days, and this is exactly how it was. We were counting minutes. We couldn't wait for those seven days to pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Ma'am, are you certain -- let me ask you this: This conversation you had with VG18, was it before the event that you've described for us that you saw Mr. Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG117
utterances.text: It was before I saw Mr. Vasiljevic. This incident took place before I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam, for giving the evidence and for coming here to give it. You're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, we've got here the English version of Dr. Krstic's curriculum vitae. If I recall, there was some discussion about this at the time of the tender of the report, which is Exhibit D42. Should we add it to that as Exhibit D42.1?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think that is the best solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objection to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the curriculum vitae of Dr. Krstic will be Exhibit D42.1. Now, Mr. Domazet, I think we understand very well that you aren't able to give us any precise estimate, but can you give us at least a rough estimate of how long you need to prepare your case in response to this witness's evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, you said it right, that it is difficult for me to estimate it at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm only asking for a rough estimate. I think that we've got to have some idea of where we are headed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Especially since you said that we should finish it by Friday, if I'm not mistaken. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 4562 to 4573.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no, no. The situation we are in, as I thought I made clear after having granted the Prosecution the right to reopen its case, was that we would not finish this Friday, and that we would have to come back sometime later to hear any evidence you wish to give as the reopening of your case in answer to the last witness. All I'm asking from you is some estimate, in weeks perhaps. I think we then will have to ask to you keep in touch with us as to how you're going.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. [Interpretation] Well, I hope, especially since we have begun our preparations, Mr. Tanaskovic and I, from here, but I hope that if we were to adjourn today, then we could come -- go back to Belgrade on Thursday, and I hope that by Monday, we would have a clear idea what evidence we are going to propose, in view of the fact that the -- these witnesses also need to prepare. We need to prepare their passports, visas and so on. So it would be realistic to expect that in two weeks, we could bring these witnesses here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I think it might be more realistic if we simply say that we expect to hear from you with some idea of when you'll be able to get them here by next Tuesday or Wednesday, and then we can arrange for the Trial Chamber to sit again, and we can then set a time for the final addresses, the written addresses and the oral addresses. I'm not sure that anybody really took very much notice of my plea at the end of last year for you to start on those written submissions over your Christmas vacations, but if you didn't do it then, well then you have got plenty of time in the meantime to get the case running, getting your written submissions ready, so that there will not be much time needed for that. Very well, then, I repeat, we understand -- I think we understand the difficulties you face. We are only expecting an estimate, but we would like to have at least a progress report by next Tuesday or Wednesday and then we can get on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just one small item on this matter. I got the impression last week that it was the Defence case that it was really another person who the Defence was aware of who was working for the Red Cross who appeared to be -- appeared to look like Mr. Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Closely resembled, I think was the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Perhaps -- I was surprised in the cross-examination that the witness was never confronted with the name of that person. Perhaps to avoid having to bring her back, we could ask her to remain here tomorrow. If the Defence knows the name of this person at that time - I'm assuming they didn't know today - if they knew tomorrow the name of this person, perhaps we could, while the witness is in The Hague, just ask the Defence ask her does she know this other person?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. That would be an appropriate way. I was going to add at the very end that if, during the course of Mr. Domazet's investigations, he does come up with this sort of material, which he would want to put to this witness, then this witness will clearly have to be brought back for that purpose. But Mr. Domazet, that was the way in which you put it. If you do know who the person was, and you can put the name and even a photograph to the witness, it would best be done. We are having a lot of trouble with the translations today.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your Honour, for tomorrow, it's too early for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh, no, no. We've already said we understand that. If you don't know now, you're unlikely to know tomorrow, but clearly some notice has to be given to the Prosecution and the witness will have to be brought back for her to be confronted with some either description or name or photograph of that person, if that is to be your case. And there may be other material that you will need to put to her which you will discover only in the course of these investigations. We don't want to limit you in any way in relation to those investigations. Is there something else you wanted to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have noticed by checking that we have not admitted into evidence the report and opinion of Dr. Djurdjic, professor of criminal law, probably because we were waiting for Mr. Groome to tell us whether he wishes to cross-examine him or not. And if I remember, I think Mr. Groome said that there was no need, and that is why we didn't call him. But this written report of his has been left unadmitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think that there was some discussion about it earlier, and I pointed out that very few passages in that report are really relevant to any issue we have to determine, but that the description which he gives of the various crimes may be of some assistance to us when we look at the range of sentences to which he refers. There have been quite a few references to the former Yugoslavian law during the course of this case. We are not bound by it in any way, but we do have to pay regard to it in relation to sentencing. So what do you suggest, Mr. Groome, that we just have it tendered?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. That will make it Exhibit 47, D47. The report of was it professor?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh, yes, Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We have copies of it. I'm not sure where mine is, but I'm pretty sure we've got copies. Very well, then. On that basis, we will adjourn to a date to be fixed, but if any of you have any information about the future progress of the case, please don't hesitate to let us know. Very well. We will adjourn now.
